Publication of “Projective Verse”

The poetics essay “Projective Verse,” born of Olson's correspondence with Frances Boldereff and Robert Creeley, is published and hailed as a breakthrough by William Carlos Williams. It makes Olson the most advanced theorist of a poetics of the kinetic, the gestural, and the immediate; in it he proposes the typewritten page as a “field of action.”

Summer 1951: Williams at Black Mountain (photography, then Olson)

Drawn by Callahan, Siskind, and Shahn, Williams studies photography and learns, with Siskind's help, to use a Rolleiflex; then he enrolls in Olson's writing class, one evening a week after dinner; one memorable session runs from 7 to 11 p.m., followed by beer at Ma Peak's tavern, then back to the college for a session lasting all night and the next day, and a second evening at Peak's.

Rauschenberg paints the White Paintings
Rauschenberg makes his white canvases, which erase the figurative content and gestural trace of abstract expressionism and become the acknowledged trigger of Cage's musical silence.

On the occasion of the Gorky memorial exhibition at the Whitney, Elaine publishes a clear-sighted tribute: Gorky, tireless, maniacal, and intolerant, reduced personal tragedy to the rank of an annoyance or something unacceptable; she describes his long stride, his scowling face, his fanciful accounts of his own life, and the first impression of lightness and witty talkativeness giving way to a flow of cruel and opulent sexual imagery.
